extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and critical reasoning (general educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for detecting and avoiding common logical fallacies (false analogy, ambiguity, illicit conversion, bad generalization, syllogistic errors, etc.) in argumentation and scientific reasoning. Emphasizes exposing suppressed premises, preserving qualifications, and testing analogies and metaphors by showing causal parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Analogy / bad analogical inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer properties (especially causal or essential ones) in one case merely from similarity in many respects between two cases; an analogy proves nothing unless the applicability (that the same law is operating) is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that in the two cases asserted to be analogous the same law or causal connection is really operating; prove by just induction or render probable that the case resembles the set of analogous cases in the circumstances on which the disputed question hinges. Examples: Pythagoreans' 'music of the spheres', the metropolis/heart analogy, and the false inference that more size = disease. Beware of drawing inferences from superficial resemblances (e.g., number 'perfections' applied to planetary count).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor is not proof; must establish applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: A metaphor or figurative illustration is not an argument by itself; it asserts that an argument exists and is useful chiefly to aid apprehension and suggest a proof, but its applicability must be demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors to clarify what is to be proved and to suggest the means of proof, but do not treat them as evidence. Check parity of relations between metaphor source and target (e.g., agricultural illustration of mental cultivation has logical value only if the same grounds apply). Beware poor metaphors that lack parity of cause (e.g., Bacon's 'river carries froth and straws' used as proof without causal similarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization / bad classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid forming broad general propositions from classes that have no common properties or only trivial commonalities; bad classification is a fertile source of false generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not group heterogeneous items under one name and then assert general propositions about the group; make sure the defining properties are substantial enough to support induction. Example: ancient notions like 'Humidum' covered many unrelated actions and produced abortive philosophizing. Be cautious when extending a commonplace term by slight links of connection to dissimilar cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of Ambiguity (ambiguous terms / shifting senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors arise when a word true in one sense is reasoned on as if true in another sense; ambiguity in middle terms or terms used in different senses in premises and conclusion leads to fallacious reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure terms keep a consistent meaning throughout an argument. Watch for ambiguous middle terms, paronymous (conjugate) words assumed equivalent, and etymological fallacies. Examples: 'money' (currency vs capital), 'representative' (literal spokesperson vs legally responsible representative), 'theory' (completed induction vs mere speculation), 'church' (clergy vs whole body of believers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paronymous-word fallacy / Fallacia Figuræ Dictionis
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume paronymous or grammatically related words have precisely corresponding meanings (e.g., art vs artful; design vs designing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether small grammatical or morphological changes alter meaning in a way that undermines the supposed equivalence. Examples: 'projectors are unfit to be trusted; this man has formed a project' — illicitly treating 'project' and 'projector' as equivalent. Also watch for non-correspondence between 'presume' and 'presumption'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etymological fallacy (using original/etymological sense incorrectly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid asserting that a term's original or etymological sense fixes its proper current meaning and therefore supports an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on customary/legal/current sense determined by usage and context rather than etymology. Example: using the etymological sense of 'represent' to argue that an MP must be a mere mouthpiece of constituents, ignoring legal/customary meaning requiring independent judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illicit conversion and invalid oppositions (converse errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not perform simple conversion of universal affirmatives (All A are B → All B are A) or accept the invalid converse of hypothetical propositions (If A then B ≠ If B then A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize correct logical converses: from If A then B the valid inference is 'If not B then not A' (contrapositive), not 'If B then A.' Avoid treating a true conclusion as proof of the truth of premises (mistaking consequence for antecedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing contrary and contradictory propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mistake the contrary of a proposition for its contradictory; contrary propositions may both be false while contradictories cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish logical oppositions properly; forcing an argument to express itself explicitly will help detect this error. Example: mistaking the reverse of wrong for right in conduct is a practical form of this logical error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic fallacies (undistributed middle, illicit process, extra terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vicious syllogisms typically involve more than three terms, an undistributed middle, or illicitly distributing a term; such formal errors invalidate deductive reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make premises explicit and test the syllogistic form: the rules of syllogism expose these defects. While suppressed premises often make diagnosis subtle, requiring explicit statement of premises forces the reasoner to defend them or reveal a hidden falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing premises between linked arguments (à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not drop qualifications, limitations, or necessary conditions that were attached to a premise when using it later in an argument; applying a 'secundum quid' (qualified) proposition 'simpliciter' (absolutely) is fallacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve qualifications (conditions of time, circumstance, or other provisos) when transferring premises into new parts of an argument. Examples: Mercantile theory misapplies 'whatever brings in money enriches' without the proviso about the ability to employ money; arguments about tithes, colonization policy, and prices 'finding their level' often drop temporal or conditional qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misapplication of abstract truths (treating 'true in the abstract' as absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reasoning from principles that are true only when modifying causes are absent as if they were true in all circumstances without exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and account for the modifying causes or background conditions that make an abstract principle valid; when such conditions may exist in practice, do not treat the abstract truth as universally applicable. The text notes this is especially dangerous in politics and social questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous middle or grammatical-structure fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors arise when grammatical structure or shifts in wording create the appearance of a logical connection that does not exist (e.g., assuming exact correspondence across parts of speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether changes for grammatical convenience preserve meaning; if not, the argument may rely on Fallacia Figuræ Dictionis or shifting senses. Examples: 'murder should be punished with death; this man is a murderer, therefore he deserves to die' is acceptable only because meanings align; similar but non-equivalent shifts produce fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about suppressed premises and the conditions of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments often rely on unspoken premises or forgotten reasons that, if articulated, reveal necessary limitations; exposing these suppressed premises clarifies whether conclusions legitimately follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compel arguers to state their full premises; consider what conditions (time, competing causes, institutional arrangements) justify a proposition before using it as a premise. The rules of syllogism and making premises explicit are effective protections against many fallacies described.
